newsitem.title: USA: U.S. looking for signal from China on WTO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. looking for signal from China on WTO.

text.p: U.S. officials said Thursday they will be looking for indications from China in upcoming high level meetings that Beijing is ready to negotiate in earnest on joining the World Trade Organisation.

"With respect to the WTO, we of course will be looking for signals," Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord said at a news conference on Secretary of State Warren Christopher's upcoming trip to China.

"There will not be detailed negotiations; we don't have that kind of team here," he added. "But it will be a very important part of our agenda -- both because China's interested in it and because we would like to see them become a member of the WTO."

U.S. officials said the tone of negotiations with China on the WTO has improved significantly in recent weeks and noted Beijing's recent promise to make any new trade policies consistent with the rules of the global trading system.

But U.S. officials say they are still looking for Beijing to signal a willingness to undertake the kinds of economic reforms and market opening moves the United States and its key trading partners feel are a necessary condition of China's entry into the WTO.

U.S. officials say reforms are necessary because without them the huge and rapidly growing Chinese economy could upset the global trading system. Also they feel that the rules under which China enters the WTO will set a precendent for other countries eager to join the global trading forum.

U.S. officials have been disappointed that China has not signalled more of a willingness to engage in serious negotiations despite efforts by Washington to show new flexibility. Part of the problem, they said, is that some of the reforms needed would expose heavily subsidised, inefficient, money losing state enterprises to tough foreign competition.

"We recognise they've got some challenges and we're willing to be flexible in certain areas," Lord said. "But, they have got to come forth with a more meaningful arrangement. And hopefully, we'll get better signals from them while we're there."

Christopher arrives in Beijing on November 19 for meetings with President Jiang Zemin and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen to lay the groundwork for a meeting between President Clinton and Jiang on November 24 during the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders meeting in Manila, Philippines.

The United States has some specific trade irritants, such as wheat and curbs on information flows, it wants Beijing to address and is looking for more concrete commitments on basic rules of trade and market access issues, officials said.
China could at the APEC meeting announce a round of import tariff reductions on about 2,000 items in addition to cuts on thousands of items already announced, U.S. officials said.

But it is unlikely that Clinton and Jiang will engage in detailed discussions during their meeting or come out with anything concrete from the meeting on the WTO issue, said one administration official.

"What we are looking for is to let President Jiang know that we think the discussions are productive and that they are moving in the right direction but to emphasise that it is important for China to come back to the table prepared to make the kind of commitments that we and other countries have been talking about," the official said.
"Once the negotiations really get started in earnest they can actually proceed quite expeditiously," he added.
